title: Let no one say it truly
hook: let no one be able to say truly that you aren't simple or good (Meditations 10.32)

segments.voice: Yesterday: second edge Your line was is it this. What did your three answers sort? Day six hundred nineteen.

Someone says something about you behind your back. Selfish, they say, or fake, or lazy. It stings, and it's easy to end up arguing with them in your head, in the shower, on the drive. But there's a quieter question underneath the sting: is it true? Marcus doesn't tell himself to stop people from talking. He tells himself something harder, and much more in his control. Today: two questions.
screen: `SAID BEHIND YOUR BACK.` → `ARGUING IN THE SHOWER.` → `LET NO ONE SAY IT TRULY.`

segments.voice: First, the line. Let no one be able to say truthfully of you, Marcus writes, that you are not simple, or not good. Let anyone who thinks that of you be a liar. Second, the shift. He isn't trying to control what people say. People will say what they say. He's trying to control whether it's true. You can't stop the rumor. You can make it false. Third, it's in your power. All of this, he writes, is up to you. Who can stop you from being good and simple? No one. Other people can mislabel you, but they can't make the label stick to the person you actually are. Fourth, the test it gives. This turns criticism into something useful. When a remark lands, there are two questions. Is it true? If it isn't, it's their mistake, and you can let it go. If it is, even a little, then you've just been handed a free piece of information, and the work is to make it false, starting today. Either way, the energy goes into living, not into defending. And notice the two words he picks again: simple and good, the same pair book ten opened with, when he asked his soul whether it would ever be good and simple. A few pages later, he's still working on it.
screen: `LET THEM BE WRONG ABOUT YOU.` · `YOU CAN'T STOP THE RUMOR.` · `WHO CAN STOP YOU BEING GOOD?` · `TRUE? THEN MAKE IT FALSE.` · then, large: `LET IT BE FALSE.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one criticism you've heard about yourself, or one you're afraid of. Hold it up to the light. Is there any truth in it? Be honest, and gentle. If there's none, set it down. If there's some, picture one act today that would make it false: the generous thing for selfish, the plain thing for fake, the finished thing for lazy. See yourself doing it. The bell holds the time.
Two questions. Marcus's test for criticism: is it true, and if so, what will you do to make it false. Today's word.
Your line: let it be false. Pick one criticism, fair or unfair, and act today so that it isn't true. Day six hundred nineteen.

howItsDone: People who use this passage often answer criticism by first asking whether it's true, and if any part is, by quietly changing that part rather than arguing.

pairs: what Marcus wants no one to deny

myth: Marcus tells himself to make people stop criticizing him
he aims to make the criticism false, not to silence it.
he says being simple and good is in your own power
who can stop you from being good and simple? he asks.

fork.setup: you hear that someone called you fake. you're Marcus. what do you do?
options: confront them and demand they take it back.
ask whether it's true, and live so that it isn't.
fork.reveal: let no one be able to say truly that you aren't simple or good, he writes; let whoever thinks it be a liar. that part is in your power.

original.note: Greek: truly, truthfully. Marcus wants no one to be able to name his faults alēthōs.

trapdoor: what you thought: don't care what people think.
what it means: you can't stop what people say, but you can make sure it isn't true.
what a scholar hears: simple and good, the pair Marcus uses here, also opens book ten, where he asks his soul whether it will ever be good and simple.

notes: 10.32 paraphrased (Long: 'Let it not be in any man's power to say truly of thee that thou art not simple or that thou art not good; but let him be a liar whoever shall think anything of this kind about thee; and this is altogether in thy power. For who is he that shall hinder thee from being good and simple?'). Confirm.
10.32 continues 'Only do thou determine to live no longer, unless thou shalt be such'; the script omits this clause deliberately. A Keeper may wish to confirm.
Editor review (year 2): removed the 'first thing most of us do' claim from the hook and the trapdoor's unsourced 'one of his recurring ideals'; the trapdoor now points to 10.1, which is cited.
